title: The fiftieth listener (Kern ch. 17)
hookLine: even the fiftieth person to hear it passed on, rejoicing, has great merit

cards: A recipe card sits in a kitchen drawer, butter-stained at one corner, in an aunt's handwriting. She copied it from a neighbor, who copied it from someone nobody in the family ever met. Nobody in that chain was a chef.
Each simply liked it enough to hand it on, and somewhere along the way a pinch of something got added.
Chapter seventeen of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, follows a chain like that, link by link, then asks a surprising question about the person at the very end.

teach.b: First, the question. Maitreya asks what merit comes to someone who hears this teaching and rejoices in it. The Sanskrit word is anumodana: rejoicing, being glad along with someone.
Not doing anything yet. Just being glad.
Second, the chain. Someone hears the teaching in an assembly, goes off to a village or town, and tells it as well as they can remember to a friend or relative.

That person is glad, and tells another, who tells another, on and on, until it reaches a fiftieth person, who hears it at the far end of all that retelling, perhaps a little blurred, and rejoices too.

Beside that fiftieth listener stands a great patron who gives countless beings everything they could want for many years, then teaches them until they reach the highest fruits of the path. That patron's merit is enormous.
And yet, the Buddha says, the fiftieth listener's gladness is greater, beyond counting. And if that is true of the fiftieth, how much more of the first. Fourth, the small acts.

The chapter goes on, almost tenderly: someone who goes to hear the teaching for a little while, someone who says to a friend, come and listen with me, someone who moves over and offers part of their seat to a newcomer.
Each is honored. The teaching doesn't wear thin as it travels hand to hand. The gladness travels with it, and arrives whole.

how: In schools that honor the Lotus Sutra, people rejoice in hearing it, invite others to listen, and pass its teaching on; the chapter's picture of a chain of glad hearers is read as encouragement to share the teaching, however secondhand.

o: the last disciple the Buddha taught before he died
a monk who listens to the sutra fifty times over
the one at the end of a long chain of telling, still glad

games.q: the fiftieth listener: tap the pairs.
p: hears it secondhand, and is glad
gives beings all they could want
one of the small acts honored

s: in this chapter, a teaching heard fiftieth-hand is worth little
the fiftieth listener's gladness is called greater than the great patron's gift.
the chapter honors someone who invites a friend to come and listen
it names small acts: going to hear, inviting a friend, sharing a seat.
the sutra calls the great patron's merit small
it agrees the patron's merit is enormous, and still weighs the gladness higher.

games.q: you heard the teaching from a friend, who heard it from someone else, fifty links back. it may be a little blurred. what does the sutra say about your gladness in it?
o: it counts for little, so far from the source
it only counts if you repeat it word for word
games.why: the Buddha says even the fiftieth listener's gladness outweighs a great patron's gift; and how much more, he adds, the first hearer's.

practice: Name, quietly, one good thing that reached you through someone else, a book, a kindness, a way of making tea, and trace it back a link or two if you can. Then picture one person you could hand it to, and see them receiving it.
Rest there, with the chain one link longer.

wordCard.voice: The fiftieth listener. In the Lotus Sutra, the one at the end of a long chain of telling, whose simple gladness still carries great merit. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: rejoicing, being glad along with someone; the key word of this chapter.

carryVoice: Your line: passed on and on. Gladness doesn't wear thin on the way. Back tomorrow, same hill.
